title: Data Manipulation: Runtime Data Manipulation
summary: Runtime Data Manipulation changes what a user or a process sees when data is read, without altering the stored record itself. The adversary normally edits the application that presents the information: a patched binary, a swapped dynamic library, a replaced reporting script, or a shim loaded ahead of the real component. A related route is changing file associations so that opening a data file launches a different program, or masquerading a tool under a trusted name. The stored value stays truthful, which is why database level integrity checks and backups look clean and only the presentation layer lies. Artefacts include unexpected modification of application binaries on reporting servers, unsigned or newly signed modules loaded by a reporting service, changes to file association registry keys, and process creation where a reporting tool starts from an unusual parent process. Defenders separate this from legitimate patching by tracking approved change windows, publisher signatures and file hashes for the reporting stack.

beginner.definition: Data manipulation means changing information so that it no longer matches reality. This version leaves the stored files alone and changes the program that reads and shows them. The real numbers stay correct in the database underneath, but the screen, report or export is wrong. It works because people trust the software that presents the facts.
beginner.whyItMatters: People make decisions from screens and reports, not from raw databases. If the display is quietly wrong, staff may approve a payment, release a shipment or sign off an inspection that should have failed. Because the stored data is untouched, backups and audits often look normal. The business may learn the truth much later, when a customer complains or an outside auditor checks the figures.
howItWorks: The attacker gains access to the server or workstation that runs the reporting or display software.
They replace or patch a program file, library or script so that it hides or alters certain values.
They may also change file associations, so that opening a report launches a program they control.
When staff open the report, the modified program reads the true data and shows a false version.
Audit checks inside the database still pass, because the stored records themselves were never changed.
The tampering is found later by comparing file hashes or signatures with a known good copy.
beginner.example: Picture a shop where the till prints the daily sales summary. A thief does not touch the stock room or the sales records at all. Instead, they swap the small program that prints the summary, so that it always prints a slightly lower total. The real sales are still in the system, and every audit of the sales data is clean. The owner only notices when the money in the drawer does not match what the shelves should have earned.
takeaways: The stored data and the displayed data can disagree, so check the file that produces the report.
Watch for changed binaries, libraries and file associations on the machines that build reports.
Keep a known good hash or signature for reporting software so that tampering becomes visible.

objectives: Describe how runtime data manipulation changes the display rather than the stored record.
Explain how modified application binaries or libraries can falsify what a user sees.
Identify the log and file integrity sources that reveal a changed reporting component.
Distinguish an approved software update from an unauthorised change to a reporting tool.
Explain why database level integrity checks may still pass during this kind of attack.
